paras: The Holdenville hotel dynamiting was a bomb attack on the quarters of Black hotel workers in Holdenville, Indian Territory, on the night of Saturday, January 24, 1903, after the workers had been ordered to leave the town. No one was reported hurt, but the workers left on the first train out, and the dispatches tied the attack to a local rule that no Black people should live in the town. Papers in Kansas and Indian Territory carried the story within a week, one under the headline "Serious Race Trouble."

According to a Holdenville dispatch printed in the Daily Ardmoreite, there was "an unwritten law" in the town that no Black people should live there. The need for domestics and hotel help had nonetheless led to the employment of a limited number of Black workers, and "dire threats" had been made against them and against those who employed them. The Wichita Daily Eagle's dispatch said that Black help had been hired at some of the hotels a few days earlier, that a strong sentiment was expressed at once against the hotel keepers, and that the workers were then ordered to leave town but did not go.

At about 11 o'clock on Saturday night, according to the Eagle, "some miscreant" threw a dynamite bomb against a small building behind one of the hotels that served as servants' quarters, smashing its windows. The Ardmoreite's dispatch named the target as the habitation of the Hotel Scott and described a much larger blast that rocked many buildings in the business section and broke many windows. The Black workers, "terrified" in the Ardmoreite's word, left town on the first outgoing train.

The blast also set off a false alarm: an armed guard had escorted a Frisco train through that evening, and many townsmen seized revolvers and Winchesters and ran to the bank expecting to find outlaws looting it. Neither dispatch names the bomber, and no arrest for the bombing appears in the coverage.

On Sunday, the day after the bombing, a party of Black women working as domestics was accosted on the street, the Ardmoreite reported. The man accused was arrested and tried in the commissioner's court on Tuesday on a charge of using "vile and indecent language"; the coverage does not give the verdict. The prosecution was backed by a number of the town's leading men, who had decided to defend their domestic help "despite the violent opposition of the community."

A Black paper later described the town in the same terms: in May 1903 a traveling agent for the Western World wrote that it was "a town where not a colored person lives" and that "poor white riffians" harassed the party as they changed trains there.

White papers in Kansas and Indian Territory reported the bombing between January 29 and 31, 1903. The Wichita Daily Eagle ran the Holdenville dispatch on its front page under the headlines "Dynamite Frightens Negroes" and "Bomb Fired to Get Them Out of Holdenville," giving as much space to the town's fear of a bank robbery as to the attack. Its closing line said citizens congratulated themselves that the worst damage "was the loss of the negro help and a few broken window glasses." The same issue's "Outlines of Oklahoma" column reduced the story to three lines ending with the workers having "went a-flying," and the Chickasha Daily Express reprinted that item word for word two days later.

The Daily Ardmoreite headed its dispatch "Serious Race Trouble" and called the bombing a "violent expression" of community sentiment. Yet the same dispatch ended by saying the trouble was "not a question of race, but a question of competent domestic help." No Black-press report of the bombing was found; the Western World's traveling letter mentioned Holdenville only as a town without Black residents.

The two dispatches differ on the target: the Eagle described a bomb thrown against a small servants' building behind an unnamed hotel, while the Ardmoreite named the Hotel Scott and said that "one or two of the domestics were dynamited," though neither reports anyone injured. The Ardmoreite's account also leaves unclear whether every Black worker left, since it reports Black domestics accosted on the street the day after the "colored contingent" fled.

reader.title: Holdenville hotel dynamiting
bases: Black hotel workers were ordered to leave town, a dynamite bomb was set off at their quarters to drive them out, and they left on the first train (A1, A3).

Two separately worded Holdenville dispatches, dated Jan. 28 and Jan. 29, agree that Black hotel workers ordered out of town had their quarters dynamited on Saturday night and then left (A1, A3); A2 and A4 derive from A1.

accounts.label: Holdenville dispatch, Wichita Daily Eagle
accounts.gist: Black help hired at the hotels were ordered out and failed to go; 'some miscreant' threw a bomb against their small quarters behind a hotel, breaking windows, and they took the first train; the town briefly feared a bank hold-up.

accounts.label: Holdenville dispatch, Daily Ardmoreite
accounts.gist: An unwritten law barred Black residents; after threats, the habitation of the Hotel Scott was dynamited in a blast that rocked the business section, and the Black workers fled; leading men then backed the prosecution of a man who accosted Black domestics.

accounts.label: Black travelers' letter
accounts.gist: Four months later a Western World agent described Holdenville as a town with no Black residents where whites harassed Black travelers changing cars.

framing.detail: Headlined 'Dynamite Frightens Negroes / Bomb Fired to Get Them Out of Holdenville'; calls the bomber a 'miscreant' but dwells on the feared bank robbery and counts 'the loss of the negro help' as the worst damage.
Three-line column item saying the workers 'went a-flying' after dynamite was thrown under their quarters, without comment.
Reprints the Eagle's column item word for word.
Headlined 'Serious Race Trouble'; calls the bombing a 'violent expression' and an 'outbreak' but concludes it is 'not a question of race, but a question of competent domestic help.'
No Black-press report of the bombing was found; a later traveling letter calls Holdenville's white harassers 'poor white riffians.'
